screens.title: RHCE Exam Overview & Preparation Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson we'll frame what the RHCE exam requires and how to prepare so your practice mirrors the test. The RHCE exam, EX294, is performance-based: you work in a live Red Hat Enterprise Linux environment and complete practical tasks rather than answering multiple-choice questions. This structure verifies that you can automate real administrative tasks reliably. You will often have three to four hours to finish a set of objectives; that means accuracy and speed both matter. Ansible automation is central: the exam checks your ability to configure Ansible, manage inventories, author playbooks, and use modules to reach a desired system state across multiple machines. To prepare effectively, set up a small VM lab with a control node and one or more managed nodes, practice tasks end-to-end, validate results, and rehearse under time limits. Common pitfalls include misreading task details, YAML indentation mistakes, forgetting to use become for privilege escalation, or missing SSH key setup. As you go through this chapter, think about one specific area you feel weakest in and plan a focused lab exercise to build confidence.

screens.title: Performance-Based Exam Explained
screens.narratorSegment: A performance-based exam requires you to perform tasks in a live environment rather than select answers. That means success is demonstrated through action: configuring systems, running commands, and validating results. For RHCE EX294 this translates into working in a RHEL environment and completing automation tasks, often across multiple hosts, within a time limit. A concrete example is a task that asks you to ensure a web server package is installed and serving on a specific port across a host group. You must configure the package, start the service, adjust firewall rules if necessary, and verify connectivity. A common misconception is that rote memorization of commands is sufficient; in reality the exam rewards automation, planning, and verification. Another contrast is multiple-choice tests, which assess recognition and recall; performance-based tests assess synthesis and application. To prepare, practice whole tasks end-to-end: plan the steps, execute with Ansible, and always verify the desired state. A final takeaway: treat each task as a small project—read it carefully, plan, execute, verify, and document assumptions. What small project will you practice first in your lab? screens.title: Ansible Automation: Control Node and Managed Nodes
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible's model centers on a control node that orchestrates actions and one or more managed nodes that receive tasks. The control node runs playbooks and opens SSH sessions to managed nodes; managed nodes execute modules and return results. In the RHCE exam you will use this pattern to apply changes consistently across hosts. A practical example: your control node has an inventory grouping web servers; a playbook targets that group to install and start a web service. A common misconception is that Ansible requires agents on managed nodes — it does not; it uses SSH and modules. Another important point is inventory structure: host groups let you target sets of machines efficiently and avoid repetitive tasks. For exam readiness, ensure your control node can reach managed nodes without password prompts by configuring SSH keys and creating a sudo-enabled non-root user on targets. Finally, document how your inventory maps to lab VMs and verify connectivity with a simple ping module run before attempting task changes. What connectivity or inventory detail will you verify first in your lab? screens.title: Idempotency and Module Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Idempotency means applying the same operation multiple times results in the same system state as applying it once. In the context of Ansible, modules are designed to be idempotent so playbooks can be rerun safely. For example, an idempotent package task will install a package only if it is not already present; running it again does not reinstall the package. This property is crucial in the exam: you may need to run a playbook multiple times while refining it, and idempotency ensures you do not create unintended side effects. A common misconception is that all commands are idempotent—shell or command tasks can be non-idempotent unless you guard them with checks. When possible, prefer built-in modules such as the package or service modules because they include state checks. A practical tip is to run a task twice during practice to confirm it reports no changes the second time. The core takeaway: design playbooks that reach and confirm the desired state without causing repeated changes, and when you cannot avoid shell commands, add guards that make the step idempotent. content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Idempotency
Idempotency Explained
How Ansible modules ensure safe repeatable changes.
Definition
An operation that, when applied multiple times, yields the same result as applying it once.
Example
Package installation task
Using a package module that ensures 'state: present' will install only if missing, not on every run.
Contrast
Module vs shell command
Shell commands may be non-idempotent unless you add explicit checks; prefer modules when possible.
Key Takeaway

Design playbooks so they can be run repeatedly without causing unexpected changes; test by running tasks twice.

Practical Checks
  • Use module state parameters such as state: present or state: started.
  • Run the same playbook twice and observe the second run reports no changes when idempotent.
  • If a shell step is required, add condition checks to avoid repeated effects.
Pro tip
Prefer fully qualified module names for clarity and future compatibility when writing playbooks for the exam.

screens.title: YAML Syntax and Common Playbook Errors
screens.narratorSegment: YAML is the syntax used to author Ansible playbooks and it's sensitive to indentation and structure. A small mistake like a misplaced space can change a mapping into a scalar or cause a parser error. For example, forgetting to align task keys or mixing tabs and spaces will make a playbook fail before execution. A frequent misstep in the exam is assuming a task ran when in fact Ansible skipped it due to wrong indentation. To avoid these problems, validate YAML before running playbooks and keep consistent two-space indentation. Use clear, minimal playbooks in the exam: explicit hosts:, become: yes when required, and properly nested tasks and modules. A concrete practice: write a short play that installs a package and run a YAML linter locally, then execute the play and watch for structure-related errors. Remember the contrast: shell commands are forgiving to formatting in the shell itself, but YAML must be precise. Closing question: when you next write a playbook, which YAML structure will you check first to prevent common failures? content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › YAML & Playbook Errors
YAML Syntax Essentials
Common sources of playbook failures and how to prevent them.
Best practices
  • Use two-space indentation consistently and never use tabs.
  • Always include hosts: and necessary become: yes where privileged tasks are required.
  • Validate YAML with a linter before running on managed nodes.
Misconception
Formatting is cosmetic
Formatting mistakes are functional errors in YAML; they can prevent a playbook from running or produce unexpected behavior.
Code Walkthrough
---
- name: Install and start httpd
  hosts: webservers
  become: yes
  tasks:
    - name: Ensure httpd is installed
      ansible.builtin.yum:
        name: httpd
        state: present
    - name: Ensure httpd is started
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: httpd
        state: started
Checklist
  • Confirm indentation aligns module arguments under the module name.
  • Use the correct module name for your RHEL version (for example, dnf or yum variation may be tested).
  • Validate before running and run with increased verbosity when troubleshooting.

screens.title: Exam Time Management & Strategy
screens.narratorSegment: Time management in a performance-based exam is a practiced skill. Start by quickly scanning all tasks to understand scope and to identify easy wins and time-consuming items. Allocate your time: pick low-effort tasks first to secure points, then tackle larger automation items with more planning. For each task follow a repeatable process: read the requirement fully, outline the steps to reach the desired state, implement a focused playbook or change, and verify the outcome with concrete checks. A common mistake is rushing to implement before reading details like specific port numbers or file permissions; that costs points. Use a timer during lab practice to build a sense for realistic pacing and practice partial completion strategies—complete as much of a complex task as possible and clearly document what remains. Another effective habit is to validate after each task rather than saving verification for the end; this avoids compounded errors. Finally, reflect after each practice run: note recurring time sinks and refine your approach. What small adjustment could shave minutes off your next practice run? screens.title: Designing a Minimal VM Lab
screens.narratorSegment: A minimal but effective lab mirrors the control and managed node relationship you will use in the exam. Plan for at least two VMs: one control node with Ansible installed and one managed node as the target. Choose RHEL 8 or 9 as used in practice tasks. Ensure network connectivity between VMs and configure SSH keys for passwordless authentication from the control node to the managed node. Create a non-root user on both machines and grant sudo on the managed node to that user. A concrete example setup sequence is: install the OS on both VMs, install Ansible on the control node, generate an SSH key pair on the control node, copy the public key to the managed node’s authorized_keys, and verify SSH access. A common pitfall is assuming SSH works without checking for correct permissions on the. ssh directory or authorized_keys file; incorrect file permissions can block key-based authentication. Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Lab Design
Minimal Lab Plan
Steps to create a reproducible test environment for practice.
  1. Provision two VMs with RHEL 8 or 9: one control node and one managed node.
  2. Install Ansible on the control node and create a project directory for playbooks.
  3. Create a non-root user on both machines and grant sudo on the managed node.
  4. Exchange SSH keys to enable passwordless authentication from the control node.
  5. Verify connectivity and run a simple ping or a module check.
Command Callouts
Sample commands and verification patterns for lab setup.
# On control node: generate key and copy to managed node
ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 2048 -f ~/.ssh/id_rsa
ssh-copy-id user@managed-node

# Verify passwordless SSH
ssh user@managed-node 'echo OK'

# Run a simple Ansible ping from control node
ansible all -i inventory.ini -m ansible.builtin.ping -u user --become
Watchouts
  • Check .ssh directory and authorized_keys permissions; too-permissive or too-restrictive permissions can prevent key auth.
  • Ensure the sudoers entry allows the non-root user to run required tasks with become.

screens.title: SSH Key Setup and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Passwordless SSH is critical for running Ansible playbooks without interruptions. The basic flow is: generate a key pair on the control node, copy the public key to the managed node’s authorized_keys, and confirm you can SSH without a password. In practice, failures often come from incorrect file permissions, missing public key entries, or user mismatch. An example problem is copying the key for root but attempting to connect as a non-root user; the mismatch prevents access. Troubleshooting steps include verifying that the authorized_keys file contains the expected public key, checking that the. ssh directory has permissions 700 and the authorized_keys file has permissions 600, and testing SSH with the verbose flag to see authentication steps. On the exam, if SSH fails, do not panic: check user names, permissions, and whether SSH agent forwarding or wrong key files are in use. Practicing these checks until they become muscle memory will reduce time lost during the exam. Which SSH verification step will you practice until it becomes automatic? screens.title: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: There are recurring errors candidates make that are easy to prevent with simple checks. ---
- name: Create deploy user

        groups: deploygroup

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson we'll frame what the RHCE exam requires and how to prepare so your practice mirrors the test. The RHCE exam, EX294, is performance-based: you work in a live Red Hat Enterprise Linux environment and complete practical tasks rather than answering multiple-choice questions. This structure verifies that you can automate real administrative tasks reliably. You will often have three to four hours to finish a set of objectives; that means accuracy and speed both matter. Ansible automation is central: the exam checks your ability to configure Ansible, manage inventories, author playbooks, and use modules to reach a desired system state across multiple machines. To prepare effectively, set up a small VM lab with a control node and one or more managed nodes, practice tasks end-to-end, validate results, and rehearse under time limits. Common pitfalls include misreading task details, YAML indentation mistakes, forgetting to use become for privilege escalation, or missing SSH key setup. As you go through this chapter, think about one specific area you feel weakest in and plan a focused lab exercise to build confidence.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to describe the EX294 exam format and explain why it is performance-based. You will identify the key skill domains tested, with emphasis on Ansible automation, and you will be able to set up a minimal lab for realistic practice. You will also learn study strategies and common pitfalls so you can avoid preventable mistakes during the exam. Each objective targets a practical competence: knowing the format prevents time surprises; mastering Ansible playbooks and inventories ensures you can automate across machines; building a lab gives you repeatable practice; and recognizing common mistakes, like YAML indentation errors or missing privilege escalation, saves precious time on exam day. For example, being able to set up passwordless SSH between a control node and managed node is a concrete competency that directly impacts your ability to run playbooks. Think of these objectives as checkpoints: each one maps to tasks you will practice in your lab and verify during timed rehearsals.

This second objectives slide maps goals to concrete lab activities. Knowing exam format becomes a timed practice routine: simulate three to four hour sessions and score yourself by completing explicit tasks. Identifying key Ansible domains means you will practice inventory files, targeted hosts groups, writing playbooks that include become for privileged tasks, and using modules like the package and service modules. Building a lab is more than creating VMs: ensure network communication, configure SSH keys for passwordless authentication, and create a non-root user with sudo on managed nodes. Practice strategies require deliberate repetition and reflection: run a task, validate the desired state, and if it fails, use Ansible’s verbose mode and check system logs. Finally, avoid common mistakes by validating YAML before running playbooks and by using fully qualified module names when appropriate. Each objective links directly to a hands-on step you can perform and verify. As you practice, record one or two recurring errors so you can correct them systematically and build exam-ready habits.

A performance-based exam requires you to perform tasks in a live environment rather than select answers. That means success is demonstrated through action: configuring systems, running commands, and validating results. For RHCE EX294 this translates into working in a RHEL environment and completing automation tasks, often across multiple hosts, within a time limit. A concrete example is a task that asks you to ensure a web server package is installed and serving on a specific port across a host group. You must configure the package, start the service, adjust firewall rules if necessary, and verify connectivity. A common misconception is that rote memorization of commands is sufficient; in reality the exam rewards automation, planning, and verification. Another contrast is multiple-choice tests, which assess recognition and recall; performance-based tests assess synthesis and application. Ansible's model centers on a control node that orchestrates actions and one or more managed nodes that receive tasks. The control node runs playbooks and opens SSH sessions to managed nodes; managed nodes execute modules and return results. In the RHCE exam you will use this pattern to apply changes consistently across hosts. Idempotency means applying the same operation multiple times results in the same system state as applying it once. In the context of Ansible, modules are designed to be idempotent so playbooks can be rerun safely. For example, an idempotent package task will install a package only if it is not already present; running it again does not reinstall the package. This property is crucial in the exam: you may need to run a playbook multiple times while refining it, and idempotency ensures you do not create unintended side effects. A common misconception is that all commands are idempotent—shell or command tasks can be non-idempotent unless you guard them with checks. When possible, prefer built-in modules such as the package or service modules because they include state checks. There are recurring errors candidates make that are easy to prevent with simple checks. First, misreading the task is common: exam instructions are precise and often include details like exact ports, file modes, or group membership. A quick tactic is to highlight or rewrite the requirements into a checklist before starting. Second, YAML mistakes such as wrong indentation or mixing tabs will break playbooks — validate formatting before execution. Third, missing privilege escalation is frequent; remember to include become: yes when tasks need root privileges. Fourth, SSH configuration problems prevent playbooks from running at all; verify keys and permissions early. Fifth, using non-idempotent shell commands when modules exist can create inconsistent system states. To avoid these, adopt short pre-flight checks: read tasks fully, validate YAML, confirm SSH and sudo, prefer modules, and verify outcomes immediately. As a practical habit, maintain a short lab checklist you run before each practice attempt so you don’t lose time to avoidable mistakes.
